```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(weightflow)
```

A statistical office publishes **one** weight column. Every indicator, every
domain, every secondary user's table comes out of the same column: that is what
keeps a published figure internally consistent with the ones around it, and it
is why a user can compute an estimate the office never published.

The methods that make a non-probability sample usable pull the other way. Doubly
robust and machine-learning adjustments are *outcome-specific*: the best weight
for poverty is not the best weight for employment, and the literature hands you
one weight column per study variable. An office cannot disseminate that.

This article builds the reconciliation weightflow implements: a single column,
doubly robust, exactly consistent with the known population margins, that serves
every study variable at once -- and the replicate weights that let a user attach
a standard error to it. It also shows where the construction stops working, and
how the package tells you.

## The two files

Nothing here is possible without a probability **reference**: a survey that
measures the same auxiliaries as the volunteers and carries real design weights.
The two files are complementary, and neither is sufficient alone.

## A volunteer sample that is wrong in four different ways

We draw volunteers from the bundled `population` so that men and the young
over-participate, and we track four indicators of very different character: a
mean, a proportion, a **rare** proportion, and one that the selection hits head
on. None of them is used to decide who volunteers -- participation depends on
`sex` and `age` alone, which is what makes the problem correctable.

```{r frame}
set.seed(1)
pop <- population
pop$poor    <- as.integer(pop$income < quantile(pop$income, 0.12))  # ~12%: the rare one
pop$retired <- as.integer(pop$age >= 65)
N <- nrow(pop)

take <- runif(N) < plogis(-1.9 + 0.9 * (pop$sex == "M") - 0.025 * (pop$age - 45))
vol  <- pop[take, ]                                   # the volunteers: no weights at all
ri   <- sample(which(!take), 800)
ref  <- pop[ri, c("region", "sex", "age")]            # the reference: no study variables
ref$d <- N / 800                                      # its design weights

c(volunteers = nrow(vol), reference = nrow(ref))
```

```{r bias}
ind   <- c("income", "employed", "poor", "retired")
truth <- vapply(ind, function(v) mean(pop[[v]]), numeric(1))
pct   <- function(w) round(100 * (vapply(ind, function(v)
           weighted.mean(vol[[v]], w), numeric(1)) / truth - 1), 1)

pct(rep(1, nrow(vol)))        # relative bias (%) of the unweighted volunteer file
```

The unweighted file is not uniformly wrong -- it is wrong by different amounts in
different directions, which is why a single correction factor cannot fix it and
why the weight has to come from a model.

## The reference is a sample, so give it its replicates

Before anything else: the reference carries sampling error of its own, and in
this construction that error is not a detail. Every reference unit is a row of
the participation model and a row of the projection that produces the calibration
targets, so the whole weight depends on which reference units were drawn. Pass
the reference's replicate weights and the bootstrap propagates that; leave them
out and the reference is treated as the population.

In production the replicates come from the reference survey's own replicate
file. Here the reference is a simple random sample, so they can be built from
its design with the same function:

```{r refreps}
rep_ref <- bootstrap_weights(weighting_spec(ref, base_weights = d),
                             replicates = 40, seed = 11,
                             progress = FALSE)$replicates

sr <- reference_sample(ref, weights = "d", replicates = rep_ref)
```

[What it costs to skip this](#what-the-reference-contributes) is measured below.

## Step one: the pseudo-weight

`step_pseudoweight()` stacks the two files internally, fits the probability that
a unit belongs to the volunteer side rather than the reference side, and turns it
into the participation odds `(1 - p)/p`. No manual pooling, no `bind_rows()`.

```{r pseudo, warning = FALSE}
pw_only <- weighting_spec(vol, base_weights = NULL, nonprob = TRUE) |>
  step_pseudoweight(reference = sr, formula = ~ region + sex + age,
                    engine = "logit") |>
  prep()

c(sum_of_weights = sum(pw_only$final_weight), N = N)
```

That check is the one to run before going further, and it is worth knowing why.

### What the sum of the weights is telling you

Two decisions go into turning one fitted score into a weight, and both are
usually made by default rather than on purpose: whether the reference enters the
stacked file with its **design weights** or at weight one, and whether the
volunteer's weight is the **odds** `(1 - p)/p` or the plain inverse `1/p`. Neither
is visible afterwards. The margins close to numerical precision either way, no
weight looks odd, and the interval looks reasonable.

The sum of the pseudo-weights separates them, because each construction leaves a
different arithmetic trace:

<svg width="100%" viewBox="0 0 680 232" role="img" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="font-family:-apple-system,'Inter',Segoe UI,Roboto,sans-serif;">
<title>Three ways to turn one fitted score into a weight, and the trace each leaves</title>
<desc>The correct construction uses the odds with a design-weighted reference and its pseudo-weights sum to the estimated population size. Using the plain inverse adds one unit of weight per volunteer, so the sum overshoots by the volunteer share of the population. Entering the reference at weight one rescales the weights by the reference's own sampling fraction, so the sum collapses towards that fraction.</desc>

The first two are one line apart, because `1/p = (1 - p)/p + 1`:

```{r traces, warning = FALSE}
ref1 <- ref; ref1$one <- 1          # the reference stacked at weight one
pw_one <- weighting_spec(vol, base_weights = NULL, nonprob = TRUE) |>
  step_pseudoweight(reference = reference_sample(ref1, weights = "one"),
                    formula = ~ region + sex + age) |>
  prep(warn = FALSE)

round(c(odds           = sum(pw_only$final_weight) / N,
        plain_inverse  = (sum(pw_only$final_weight) + nrow(vol)) / N,
        reference_at_1 = sum(pw_one$final_weight) / N,
        n_vol_over_N   = nrow(vol) / N,
        n_ref_over_N   = nrow(ref) / N), 4)
```

The inverse overshoots by exactly the volunteer share of the population, and the
weight-one reference collapses to exactly the reference's own sampling fraction.
That is why the check has to be read **to three significant figures and before any
calibration**: afterwards the margin block imposes the population total and all
three look identical. weightflow builds the first construction, and the ratio is
in the step's diagnostics.

The distortion from stacking the reference at weight one disappears when the
reference is self-weighting, or when the calibration margins happen to span its
design strata -- so the louder mistake is the one a later step can absorb, and
the quieter one is not.

Flexible learners are available for the participation model -- `engine = "tree"`,
`"forest"`, `"boost"`, with `crossfit` -- exactly as for response propensities.

## Step two: one calibration that carries every variable

The pseudo-weight alone is consistent if the participation model is right.
A calibration is consistent if the working model for the outcome is right. Doing
both is doubly robust: correct if **either** holds.

The move that keeps it one column is to put all K study variables into the *same*
linear calibration system. Each gets its own working model -- its own predictors,
its own learner -- and the predictions enter as columns of one stacked matrix
alongside the known margins. One system, one solution, one weight.

<svg width="100%" viewBox="0 0 680 358" role="img" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="font-family:-apple-system,'Inter',Segoe UI,Roboto,sans-serif;">
<title>The multipurpose doubly robust weight as a single recipe</title>
<desc>The volunteer and reference files feed a participation model that produces the pseudo-weight. K working models, one per study variable, produce prediction columns that are stacked with the known population margins into one linear calibration. The calibration returns a single weight column used for every indicator. A band underneath shows that the replication bootstrap re-executes every step on each replicate, including the reference replicates.</desc>

In code, that whole picture is one `step_model_calibration()`:

```{r unicall, warning = FALSE}
cens <- list(sex    = as.data.frame(table(sex    = pop$sex)),
             region = as.data.frame(table(region = pop$region)))

spec <- weighting_spec(vol, base_weights = NULL, nonprob = TRUE) |>
  step_pseudoweight(reference = sr, formula = ~ region + sex + age,
                    engine = "logit") |>
  step_model_calibration(
    x_formula = ~ sex + region,          # the KNOWN margins: met exactly
    x_totals  = cens,
    models    = list(                    # one working model per study variable
      income   = y_model(income   ~ age + sex + region, engine = "glm"),
      employed = y_model(employed ~ age + sex + region, engine = "glm")),
    population = sr,
    crossfit   = 3)

fit <- prep(spec)
w   <- fit$final_weight
```

One column. Here is what it does to all four indicators -- including the two that
were never modelled:

```{r fourway}
rbind(unweighted = pct(rep(1, nrow(vol))),
      uni_weight = pct(w))
```

The two indicators with a working model are corrected, and so is `retired`, which
has none: the pseudo-weight and the margins carry it. `poor` improves least, and
that is the general pattern rather than an accident of this draw -- the cost of
sharing one weight concentrates on the rarest indicator, which is the one that
most deserves a weight of its own when the margin of error matters.

The exactness is not approximate. `prep()` records every constraint and what the
weights achieved:

```{r cons}
head(fit$steps[[2]]$diagnostics, 7)
```

## Where it stops working: the rank ceiling

Exact consistency is not free, and it does not degrade gracefully -- it is
either met or lost, for every variable at once. The reason is a rank condition.

Write `q` for the dimension of the span of the predictors the working models use
and `dim col(A)` for the number of known margins. With **linear working models
fitted in sample**, every prediction lies inside that one span, so the stacked
system can only add

<p style="text-align:center;margin:0.6em 0 1em;"><em>K &le; q &minus; dim col(A)</em></p>

variables before it becomes rank deficient. Past that point the margins are not
approximately met: they are missed.

<svg width="100%" viewBox="0 0 680 230" role="img" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="font-family:-apple-system,'Inter',Segoe UI,Roboto,sans-serif;">
<title>The rank ceiling and the two ways out of it</title>
<desc>With linear working models every prediction lies in the span of the model block, which already contains the margin block, so only q minus the dimension of the margin block directions are left for study variables. Two escapes: a richer predictor basis enlarges the span and raises the ceiling by one variable at a time, while adaptive learners and cross-fitting produce predictions outside any single fixed span, so the ceiling no longer applies.</desc>
<rect x="30" y="34" width="250" height="140" rx="10" fill="#f4f2fb" stroke="#534ab7" stroke-width="1.4"/>
<text x="155" y="54" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#3d3580">span of the model block, dim q</text>
<rect x="66" y="66" width="178" height="52" rx="8" fill="#fdf6e8" stroke="#c9902a" stroke-width="1.3"/>
<text x="155" y="88" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#5c4410">known margins</text>
<text x="155" y="106" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#8a7a50">dim col(A)</text>
<text x="155" y="140" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#4a4660">what is left for study variables:</text>
<text x="155" y="160" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="600" fill="#3d3580">q &#8722; dim col(A)</text>

<text x="480" y="48" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="#3d3580">two ways out</text>
<rect x="320" y="62" width="320" height="46" rx="8" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#9a96a8" stroke-width="1.2"/>
<text x="336" y="82" font-size="11.5" fill="#20242e">a richer predictor basis enlarges q</text>
<text x="336" y="99" font-size="11" fill="#6b6a86">the ceiling moves up, and binds again one variable later</text>
<rect x="320" y="118" width="320" height="56" rx="8" fill="#eaf5f0" stroke="#1d9e75" stroke-width="1.3"/>
<text x="336" y="138" font-size="11.5" fill="#15503c">adaptive learners, or cross-fitting any model</text>
<text x="336" y="155" font-size="11" fill="#3f7a64">predictions stop lying in one fixed span,</text>
<text x="336" y="170" font-size="11" fill="#3f7a64">so the ceiling does not apply at all</text>
<text x="340" y="206" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-style="italic" fill="#8a84a8">Full rank is still not the same as well conditioned.</text>
</svg>

This is not a theoretical caution -- it happens on these 1,000 volunteers. The
margins here are `~ sex + region`, and the working models use `~ age + sex +
region`: the span has 6 directions, the margins take 5, so the ceiling is
**K = 1**. Watch the second variable break it, and watch the two escapes:

```{r ceiling, warning = FALSE}
mk <- function(ys, rhs = "~ age + sex + region")
  setNames(lapply(ys, function(v)
    y_model(as.formula(paste(v, rhs)), engine = "glm")), ys)

dev <- function(models, crossfit = NULL) {
  f <- prep(weighting_spec(vol, base_weights = NULL, nonprob = TRUE) |>
    step_pseudoweight(reference = sr, formula = ~ region + sex + age) |>
    step_model_calibration(x_formula = ~ sex + region, x_totals = cens,
                           models = models, population = sr, crossfit = crossfit),
    warn = FALSE)
  d <- f$steps[[2]]$diagnostics
  max(abs(d$achieved - d$target) / abs(d$target))   # worst constraint, relative
}

signif(c(K1              = dev(mk("income")),
         K2              = dev(mk(c("income", "employed"))),
         K2_crossfit     = dev(mk(c("income", "employed")), crossfit = 3),
         K2_richer_basis = dev(mk(c("income", "employed"),
                                  "~ age + I(age^2) + sex * region"))), 2)
```

Three of the four close to numerical zero -- that is what exact means here. `K2`
does not close at all, and the size of what it leaves on the table is not
arbitrary: the model block is constrained to totals *estimated* on the reference
while the margin block is constrained to totals *known* from the census, and the
two agree only up to the reference's sampling error. That is the shortfall you
see.

Four numbers, and they fix the specification for production: **put the known
margins in the exact-consistency block, give the working models richer
predictors, and cross-fit.** A working model that is linear in exactly the
consistency margins adds no information and breaks exactness.

## What sharing costs

Once the system is well conditioned, adding variables to it is cheap. The price
shows up in the dispersion of the weights, not in the margins:

```{r cost, warning = FALSE}
ys <- c("income", "employed", "poor", "retired")
cost <- t(vapply(seq_along(ys), function(k) {
  f <- prep(weighting_spec(vol, base_weights = NULL, nonprob = TRUE) |>
    step_pseudoweight(reference = sr, formula = ~ region + sex + age) |>
    step_model_calibration(x_formula = ~ sex + region, x_totals = cens,
                           models = mk(ys[seq_len(k)]), population = sr,
                           crossfit = 3), warn = FALSE)
  wk <- f$final_weight
  c(K = k, deff = design_effect(wk)$deff, max_min = max(wk) / min(wk[wk > 0]),
    negatives = sum(wk < 0))
}, numeric(4)))
round(cost, 2)
```

Two failure modes end that, and they look nothing alike:

- **Collinearity.** Two learners fitted to strongly correlated outcomes give
  nearly parallel prediction columns. The achieved margins start drifting from
  their targets and the package raises an ill-conditioning warning. Cross-fitting
  repairs this one.
- **Feasibility.** The margins keep closing to numerical precision while units
  start receiving *negative* weights and the weight range grows by orders of
  magnitude. Nothing in the margin diagnostics moves, and the design effect stops
  being readable as an effective sample size once negatives appear. Bounding the
  calibration repairs this one; cross-fitting does not.

So monitor the **negative count** and the **weight range** next to the margin
deviation, and treat the first negative weight as the stopping signal. Bounded
calibration together with cross-fitting is the production default.

## What the reference contributes {#what-the-reference-contributes}

Now the arm we set up at the start. Same recipe, same draws, same point weights;
the only difference is whether the reference enters the bootstrap with its
replicates or with its design weights alone.

```{r refvar, warning = FALSE}
sr_fixed <- reference_sample(ref, weights = "d")          # no replicates
spec_fixed <- weighting_spec(vol, base_weights = NULL, nonprob = TRUE) |>
  step_pseudoweight(reference = sr_fixed, formula = ~ region + sex + age) |>
  step_model_calibration(x_formula = ~ sex + region, x_totals = cens,
                         models = mk(c("income", "employed")),
                         population = sr_fixed, crossfit = 3)

b_full  <- bootstrap_weights(spec,       replicates = 20, seed = 2, progress = FALSE)
b_fixed <- bootstrap_weights(spec_fixed, replicates = 20, seed = 2, progress = FALSE)

c(reference_resampled = boot_mean(b_full,  "income")$se,
  reference_fixed     = boot_mean(b_fixed, "income")$se)
```

The point estimates are identical -- it is the same weight column. Only the
standard error moves, and it moves in one direction: holding the reference fixed
can only make the interval narrower, because a source of variability has been
dropped rather than estimated.

How much narrower depends on how much of the total uncertainty the reference
carries. On real household-survey structure with a reference of 800 against
1,500 volunteers, the published study behind this construction measures the
estimated standard error divided by up to **3.7**, taking a nominal 95% interval
down to **42%** coverage. Sampling error in an estimated target does not announce
itself as an unmet constraint, which is where an office would look for it.

`bootstrap_weights()` now says so when the replicates are missing, and
`jackknife_weights()` says something stronger: a delete-one replicate has no
reference replicate to pair with, so it holds the reference fixed whatever you
pass. For this construction, use the bootstrap.

## Dissemination

The replicate weights are the deliverable, not just the point column. For a
non-probability source they are the only way a secondary user can attach a
standard error to an estimate the office never published.

```{r disseminate}
out <- collect_replicate_weights(b_full, scramble = TRUE)
c(rows = nrow(out), columns = ncol(out))
names(out)[1:4]
```

`scramble = TRUE` permutes the replicate columns so the file cannot be used to
reconstruct the resampling pattern, which is a disclosure channel in a clustered
design.

## How large is this sample, really?

A big opt-in sample can carry a small *effective* one. `data_defect()` gives the
Meng (2018) view: the error is governed by the correlation between the outcome
and participation, not by the raw count. That correlation is not observable from
the sample, so the answer is a range, not a number.

```{r datadefect}
data_defect(pw_only)
```

## Hold something out, because the weights cannot see selection bias

Double robustness protects against a misspecified model **given** ignorability,
not against its failure. If participation depends on something no model observes,
every estimator here is biased -- and the weights will not tell you. Watch:
participation now depends on income, which appears in no model and no margin.

```{r nonign, warning = FALSE}
set.seed(2)
z   <- as.numeric(scale(pop$income))                 # the driver nothing observes
t2  <- runif(N) < plogis(-1.6 + 0.8 * z)
v2  <- pop[t2, ]
r2  <- pop[sample(which(!t2), 800), c("region", "sex", "age")]; r2$d <- N / 800
sr2 <- reference_sample(r2, weights = "d")

f2 <- prep(weighting_spec(v2, base_weights = NULL, nonprob = TRUE) |>
  step_pseudoweight(reference = sr2, formula = ~ sex + age) |>
  step_model_calibration(x_formula = ~ sex,
                         x_totals = list(sex = as.data.frame(table(sex = pop$sex))),
                         models = list(income = y_model(income ~ sex + age)),
                         population = sr2, crossfit = 3), warn = FALSE)

w2 <- f2$final_weight; d2 <- f2$steps[[2]]$diagnostics
c(max_margin_deviation = max(abs(d2$achieved - d2$target)),
  negative_weights     = sum(w2 < 0),
  design_effect        = round(design_effect(w2)$deff, 2))
```

The margins are met exactly, no unit gets a negative weight, and the design
effect is unremarkable. Nothing in that line is wrong and nothing in it warns
you, which is structural rather than a shortcoming of these particular
statistics: a diagnostic built from the weights and the covariates behind them
cannot detect a dependence on a variable absent from both.

A quantity the adjustment was **never asked to reproduce** can. Here `region` is
in no model and no margin, and its population distribution is known:

```{r benchmark}
round(100 * (as.numeric(tapply(w2, v2$region, sum)) /
             as.numeric(table(pop$region)) - 1), 1)
```

Tens of per cent off, on a figure the weighted file should have reproduced for
free. Reserving one known population quantity as a held-out benchmark is the
cheapest protection available; the data-defect range above is another. Holding a
margin out in order to test against it costs precision there -- and the
alternative is a weight whose only evidence of validity is that it reproduces
what it was told to reproduce.

## The whole thing

```r
sr   <- reference_sample(ref, weights = "d", replicates = rep_ref)
spec <- weighting_spec(volunteers, base_weights = NULL, nonprob = TRUE) |>
  step_pseudoweight(reference = sr, formula = ~ age + sex + region,
                    engine = "forest") |>
  step_model_calibration(
    x_formula = ~ age + sex, x_totals = census_totals,
    models = list(
      poverty  = y_model(poverty  ~ age + sex + region + size, engine = "forest"),
      employed = y_model(employed ~ age + sex + region + size, engine = "boost")),
    population = sr, crossfit = 3)

w    <- prep(spec)$final_weight
boot <- bootstrap_weights(spec, replicates = 200)
out  <- collect_replicate_weights(boot, scramble = TRUE)
```

Seven calls: one weight column, doubly robust, exact on the census margins, with
replicate weights that propagate the participation model, the K working models
and the reference's own sampling.

## In short

1. Read the sum of the pseudo-weights against the estimated population, to three
   significant figures, **before** any calibration. It is the only point at which
   the construction is still visible.
2. Put the known margins in the consistency block; give the working models richer
   predictors and let the learner supply the non-linearity.
3. Cross-fit whenever a model is an adaptive learner. It protects coverage and it
   raises the number of variables one weight can carry.
4. Watch the negative count and the weight range, not only the margin deviation.
   The first negative weight is the stopping signal.
5. Treat the size of the reference as part of the specification, and pass its
   replicate weights -- or state that you did not.
6. Report the replication-bootstrap variance, never a fixed-total formula.
7. Hold one known population quantity out of the adjustment and test against it.
   No diagnostic computed on the weights can do that job.
8. Disseminate the replicate weights with the microdata.
